column1: # Fictitious demo data for Microsoft 365 Copilot training. Prompts are generic District Manager examples; replace bracketed text with your own context.

column6: Prompt

column3: Start of the week or the start of any day
column6: Review my email, Teams chats, and meetings from the past five business days related to my district and stores [district name or store numbers]. Group what you find by store. For each store with activity, tell me what changed, whether it needs my action, the store manager's action, or is FYI only, and cite the source. Then list the three items across the district most likely to affect customers, associates, or results this week, and flag anything that has been waiting on me for more than two days. Separate confirmed facts from possible implications.

Look at my inbox and Teams chats from the last two days. List every request from a store manager, partner team, or my leader that is waiting on me, who asked, and by when. Rank them by which store or person is blocked. For the top three, draft a short reply I can edit that answers the question, makes the decision, or sets a date. Do not send anything.
Summarize the past week in this channel by store. List requests waiting on me, open questions nobody has answered, and every deadline mentioned with the person responsible.

column3: When a large corporate or regional communication arrives
column4: Copilot Chat or Copilot in Outlook
column6: Summarize this communication for a District Manager. What changes for my stores, what do store managers need to do and by when, what do I need to decide or approve, and what questions should I expect from my store managers? Flag anything that is unclear or conflicts with earlier guidance.
column7: Add the email or file with /

column6: I am visiting [store name or number] on [day], and the store manager is [add with /]. Using my email, Teams chats, meetings, and any file I added, prepare a one-page visit brief. Include what has changed at this store in the past 30 days; commitments made at my last visit or since, with owner, due date, and status; the three metrics or conditions I should check on the walk and where in the store to look; two coaching questions for the store manager; and one thing the team has done well that I should recognize. Mark anything uncertain as Verify on the walk.

column3: On the way to the store
column6: Turn this visit brief into a walk checklist I can use on my phone: no more than 10 items, grouped by area of the store, each with what good looks like.
column7: Run as a follow-up to the visit brief

column6: Prepare me for a 1:1 with [add store manager with /]. Summarize what we discussed and agreed in the past 60 days, what is still open, wins I should recognize, and where they have asked for support. Suggest three open-ended coaching questions. Do not assess or rate the person; stick to what the content shows.

column3: Before a call with your regional leader
column6: I have a check-in with [leader] this week. Using my email, chats, and meetings from the past two weeks, draft a one-minute district update: two wins, two risks with the mitigation underway, one decision or support I need, and the stores I am most focused on and why. Cite sources.

column3: When a store manager is new to a store
column6: Using the files and messages I added, create an onboarding brief for a new store manager at [store]. Include the store's current priorities, recent results and trends, open commitments, key partner contacts, and the three things I recommend they focus on in their first 30 days.

Analyze this scorecard to show where district leadership attention would have the greatest impact this week. Rank the stores on the most recent week and on their trend across sales vs plan, availability, pickup on-time, customer satisfaction, staffing, shrink, and safety. Identify any store that looks healthy on sales but carries an operational risk, and any data-quality issues I should not trust. Show the evidence and create one chart for the most important comparison.

column3: Monthly or after a spike in complaints
column6: Analyze this customer feedback by store. Group comments into themes, quantify each theme by store and department, show where feedback worsened, and identify where store operating decisions may be creating customer problems. Include representative comments and recommend three store-level priorities.

Compare planned and actual staffed hours by store and by day of week. Identify stores and time blocks where coverage falls short during peak customer traffic, and estimate which gaps are most likely to affect pickup, availability, or checkout. Recommend where to rebalance hours first.

Using the attached shrink, sales, and customer feedback data, show whether recent loss prevention measures at [store] changed shrink, department sales, and customer satisfaction. Estimate the trade-off and list the options with the risks of each. Separate what the data shows from what needs confirmation in the store.
Argue against your top-priority store. What alternative explanation, missing data, or store context could change where I should spend my time?

Using the priorities below, draft a one-page district action plan for my store managers' weekly call. Use the sections This Week's Focus, Store Priorities (a table with store, issue, evidence, first action, owner, and check-in date), Best Practice to Adopt, Support I Will Provide, and Open Questions. Keep it direct, supportive, and specific.

column4: Copilot Chat or Copilot in Teams
column6: Rewrite this plan as a Teams post for my store managers' channel. Keep it under 150 words and readable on a phone. Lead with the one district focus, list each priority store's action and owner, recognize the best-practice store by name, and end with when we will review progress.

column3: Before a monthly or quarterly review
column6: Create a five-slide district call deck from this document: focus, store priorities, best practice, support, and next check-in. Keep one message per slide and put the supporting numbers in the speaker notes.

column3: When a store or team delivers a win
column4: Copilot Chat or Copilot in Outlook
column6: Draft a short recognition note to [store manager and team] for [achievement]. Be specific about what they did and the result, mention the associates or roles who made it happen if I have named them, and keep it under 120 words in a warm, direct tone.

Using the meeting I added, create a store-by-store commitment tracker. For each store list decisions, action items with named owner and stated due date, and support requested. Then list district-wide decisions, unresolved questions, and items discussed but not decided. Do not invent an owner or deadline; mark it Unassigned or Not specified. Then draft an Outlook email to attendees.

Review my email, chats, and meeting recaps from the past three weeks. List commitments my store managers or partner teams made to me, and commitments I made to them, that are past due or have no due date. Group by store and draft a short, friendly nudge for each that I can edit.

column4: Copilot mobile app or Copilot Chat
column6: Turn these visit notes into a recap for [store manager]: what we saw that is working, the two to three priorities we agreed, owner and due date for each, and when I will check back. Keep it under 200 words and supportive in tone.

Remember this about me for future conversations: I am a District Manager responsible for [number] stores: [store numbers and names]. My store managers are [names by store]. My key partners are [HR, loss prevention, safety, merchandising contacts]. My weekly rhythm is [district call day and time, visit days]. Default to short, phone-readable answers grouped by store, lead with what needs my action, and cite sources.

column3: Set up once and reuse every week
column6: Using only the references in this notebook, give me a store-by-store brief for this week: what changed since last week, open commitments and who owns them, the one metric to watch for each store, and the three stores I should visit first and why.
column7: Add scorecards, visit notes, and call recaps to the notebook

column6: Build a pre-read for my quarterly district review. Use my district files, meeting recaps, and email from the past 90 days to summarize results by store, the initiatives that worked and did not, and the three priorities for next quarter. Add relevant external context on customer and market trends for home improvement retail, and cite every source.
